body:
What are microorganisms?

Many living organisms are so small that they cannot be seen clearly with the unaided eye. These organisms are called microorganisms or microbes. Most are observed with the help of a microscope, which magnifies small objects.

Microorganisms are present in soil, water, air, food and the bodies of plants and animals. Some live independently, while others live on or inside another organism. They can occur in environments ranging from cold regions and deserts to hot springs and marshy lands.

Not every microorganism causes disease. Some help prepare food, produce medicines, decompose waste and maintain soil fertility. Others cause infections or spoil food.

The 5 major groups studied at school level

Microorganisms are commonly studied under bacteria, fungi, protozoa and certain algae. Viruses are considered separately because they differ fundamentally from cellular microorganisms.

1. Bacteria

Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms. They occur in numerous environments, including soil, water, milk and the human body. Many bacteria are useful, while some cause disease.

  • Lactobacillus: A useful bacterium involved in converting milk into curd.
  • Rhizobium: A bacterium associated with the root nodules of leguminous plants; it helps fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Disease-causing bacteria: Certain bacteria cause cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis.

2. Fungi

Fungi cannot prepare food through photosynthesis because they lack chlorophyll. Many obtain nutrients from dead and decaying matter. This mode of nutrition is called saprotrophic nutrition.

Some fungi are single-celled, while others are multicellular. Yeast is a single-celled fungus used in baking and fermentation. Bread mould and Penicillium are examples of mould-forming fungi. Certain mushrooms are also fungi, although their visible fruiting bodies are much larger than microscopic organisms.

3. Protozoa

Protozoa are generally single-celled organisms. Many live in water or moist environments, while some live as parasites inside other organisms.

Amoeba and Paramecium are familiar examples. Certain protozoa cause diseases: the malarial parasite Plasmodium causes malaria, while another protozoan causes amoebic dysentery.

4. Algae

Algae generally contain chlorophyll and can prepare food through photosynthesis, using light energy. They are commonly found in ponds, lakes and other moist environments.

Chlamydomonas is a microscopic, single-celled alga. Spirogyra forms multicellular green filaments that may be visible as a mass in pond water. Therefore, not all algae are microscopic.

The organisms traditionally called blue-green algae are more accurately classified as cyanobacteria. They are photosynthetic bacteria, not true algae. Some cyanobacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen.

5. Viruses

Viruses are microscopic infectious agents that differ from bacteria, fungi, protozoa and algae because they are not made of cells. A virus can multiply only inside a suitable living host cell. Its host may be an animal, plant or bacterium.

Common cold, influenza, measles, chickenpox and polio are examples of viral diseases. Bacteria can multiply independently under suitable conditions, but viruses depend on the cellular machinery of their hosts for reproduction.

Viruses are not simply another type of bacterium. Their non-cellular nature and dependence on living host cells are the essential distinctions.

Relationships between microorganisms

Some microorganisms live together in a relationship called symbiosis, in which the partners benefit from their association.

A lichen commonly contains a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga or cyanobacterium. The photosynthetic partner supplies food, while the fungus provides shelter and helps retain water and minerals.

This illustrates an important point: microorganisms may have beneficial relationships with one another, with plants and with animals.

Prelims focus

  • Lactobacillus and Rhizobium are bacteria.
  • Yeast is a single-celled fungus.
  • Amoeba and Paramecium are protozoa.
  • Chlamydomonas and Spirogyra are algae.
  • Viruses multiply only inside suitable living host cells.
  • Trap: Blue-green algae are cyanobacteria, whereas yeast is a fungus, not a bacterium.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, pp. 17–19, 2018–19; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Ch. 1, Nutrition in Plants, pp. 4–7, 2018–19; GCERT, Science, Std. 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, pp. 17–19, English-medium text.]

pictures.caption: Microorganisms are present around us, although most cannot be seen without a microscope.

pictures.alt: Four cellular microbial groups, cyanobacteria within bacteria, non-cellular viruses dependent on host cells, and lichen as a partnership.
pictures.caption: Major microbial groups and their distinguishing characteristics.

title: Microorganisms: Meaning, Major Groups and Characteristics

body:
Why are microorganisms used in food preparation?

Some microorganisms change the chemical substances present in food. Their activity can produce a desirable taste, texture or aroma. Humans have used these natural processes for preparing foods and beverages for centuries.

One important process is fermentation, in which microorganisms act on sugars and produce substances such as organic acids, alcohol or gases, depending on the organism and the conditions.

Formation of curd from milk

Curd is produced with the help of useful bacteria, especially Lactobacillus and other lactic acid bacteria.

When a small quantity of fresh curd is added to suitably warm milk, the bacteria present in that curd begin multiplying. These bacteria convert milk sugar, called lactose, into lactic acid.

The acid changes the properties of milk proteins, causing the milk to thicken and acquire the characteristic sour taste of curd.

The small quantity of curd added to fresh milk is called a starter because it introduces the useful microorganisms needed for the process.

Curd formation: Lactic acid bacteria act on milk sugar, produce lactic acid and cause milk proteins to coagulate.

Yeast and the rising of bread dough

Yeast is a single-celled fungus used in making bread and several bakery products.

Under suitable conditions, yeast uses sugars present in dough and releases carbon dioxide. Bubbles of this gas become trapped in the dough, increasing its volume and making it soft and porous.

Thus, the principal gas responsible for the rising of yeast-leavened bread dough is carbon dioxide, not oxygen or nitrogen.

Fermented Indian foods

Microbial fermentation is also involved in preparing foods such as idli, dosa, bhatura and dhokla, a familiar food in Gujarat.

Different fermented batters may contain several kinds of useful bacteria and yeasts. The microorganisms change the batter, and the gases produced during fermentation can help make the final food lighter and softer.

It is therefore incorrect to assume that every fermented food is produced by exactly the same microorganism. Curd formation mainly involves lactic acid bacteria, while baker's yeast is commonly used for bread.

Production of alcohol and vinegar

Yeast can convert sugars into alcohol during fermentation. This property is used in the production of alcoholic beverages and other fermentation products.

Microorganisms are also used to produce vinegar. In vinegar production, certain bacteria convert alcohol into acetic acid, which gives vinegar its characteristic sourness.

These examples demonstrate that microbial activity can produce different useful products, rather than having only one result.

Beneficial fermentation and unwanted spoilage

Both fermentation and microbial food spoilage involve microorganisms, but they are not equivalent.

  • Beneficial fermentation: Desired microorganisms act under suitable conditions to produce a useful food product.
  • Microbial food spoilage: Undesirable microbial activity changes food in ways that may make it unfit or unsafe for consumption.

The microorganism involved, the food material and the surrounding conditions determine whether the outcome is useful or harmful.

Prelims focus

  • Lactobacillus helps convert milk into curd.
  • Lactic acid is responsible for the sourness and thickening of curd.
  • Yeast belongs to the fungi.
  • Carbon dioxide causes yeast-leavened bread dough to rise.
  • The conversion of sugars into alcohol by yeast is fermentation.
  • Trap: Curd fermentation and bread fermentation do not depend on the same principal microorganism.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections Making of Curd and Bread and Commercial Use of Microorganisms, pp. 19–20, 2018–19; GCERT, Science, Std. 8, Ch. 2, pp. 19–20; NCERT, Health and Physical Education: A Teachers' Guide for Class 6, Unit 7, Our Environment and Health, Benefits of Microbes, p. 118, 2016.]

pictures.alt: Four illustrated flows compare bacterial curd formation, yeast-raised dough, lighter fermented batters and yeast production of alcohol.
pictures.caption: Microorganisms produce different changes in milk, dough and fermented batter.

title: Useful Microorganisms in Food: Curd, Bread and Fermentation

body:
Microorganisms as decomposers

Dead plants, fallen leaves, animal remains and other organic wastes do not simply disappear. Bacteria, fungi and other decomposers break down much of this material into simpler substances.

The process is called decomposition. It releases nutrients that can return to the soil and be used by plants.

Decomposition is important because it recycles materials already present in an ecosystem. Without decomposers, dead organic matter would accumulate and many nutrients would remain locked inside it.

Preparation of manure

In composting, suitable organic waste such as vegetable peels, leaves and plant residues is allowed to decompose. Microorganisms break down this material and contribute to the formation of compost, which can improve soil quality.

Ordinary plastics and glass do not decompose in the same way as vegetable waste. Therefore, they should not be treated as materials that readily become organic manure.

Why plants need nitrogen

Nitrogen is an essential element for living organisms. Plants use nitrogen to prepare proteins and other important substances needed for growth.

Approximately 78% of Earth's atmosphere consists of nitrogen gas. However, most plants cannot directly use atmospheric nitrogen gas. They generally absorb nitrogen from the soil in usable compounds.

Some microorganisms perform the important process of nitrogen fixation, in which atmospheric nitrogen is converted into nitrogen-containing compounds that can eventually be used by plants.

Rhizobium and leguminous plants

Rhizobium is a nitrogen-fixing bacterium that forms a beneficial association with the roots of leguminous plants.

Leguminous plants include gram, peas, beans and moong. These plants may develop small swellings called root nodules, where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live.

The relationship benefits both partners:

  • The bacteria obtain food and a suitable living environment from the plant.
  • The plant benefits from nitrogen compounds made available through bacterial nitrogen fixation.

This is an example of a symbiotic relationship.

Because legumes can obtain nitrogen through this association, growing them can contribute to soil nitrogen management. Crop rotation involving legumes may help maintain soil fertility and reduce the requirement for additional nitrogen fertiliser.

Rhizobium is a bacterium, not a fungus. Its nitrogen-fixing association is particularly associated with the root nodules of leguminous plants; it should not be assumed to occur in every crop.

Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria

Some cyanobacteria, traditionally called blue-green algae, can also fix atmospheric nitrogen. They contribute to nitrogen availability in certain soils and aquatic environments.

The ability to fix nitrogen is not shared by every bacterium or every alga. It is a property of particular microorganisms.

The nitrogen cycle

The nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen between the atmosphere, soil and living organisms.

Important processes

  1. Nitrogen fixation: Certain bacteria and cyanobacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen-containing compounds. Lightning also contributes to natural nitrogen fixation.
  2. Plant uptake: Plants absorb usable nitrogen compounds from the soil and use them to make proteins and other substances.
  3. Transfer to animals: Animals obtain nitrogen compounds by eating plants or other animals.
  4. Decomposition: Microorganisms break down dead organisms and wastes, returning nitrogen-containing substances to the soil.
  5. Denitrification: Certain soil bacteria convert nitrogen compounds back into atmospheric nitrogen gas.

These connected processes maintain the circulation of nitrogen through the environment.

Why nitrogen fixation and decomposition are different

Nitrogen fixation introduces atmospheric nitrogen into a biologically usable chemical form. Decomposition breaks down existing organic matter and recycles nutrients already present in living or dead organisms.

Both processes support soil fertility, but they are not identical.

Prelims focus

  • Atmospheric nitrogen forms approximately 78% of air.
  • Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in association with leguminous root nodules.
  • Gram, peas, beans and moong are examples of legumes.
  • Some cyanobacteria are biological nitrogen fixers.
  • Bacteria and fungi help decompose organic waste.
  • Trap: Nitrogen fixation and denitrification are opposite processes in the nitrogen cycle.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, sections Increasing Soil Fertility, Cleaning the Environment, Nitrogen Fixation and Nitrogen Cycle, pp. 21–27, 2018–19; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Ch. 1, Nutrition in Plants, section How Nutrients Are Replenished in the Soil, p. 7; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 1, Crop Production and Management, pp. 2, 5–7.]

pictures.caption: Microbial decomposition helps return nutrients from organic waste to agricultural soil.
